newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: African states commit to privatisation.
newsitem.headline: African states commit to privatisation.

text.p: Southern African nations are committed to embracing the private sector and selling off their state-owned assets, but the process is set to be long and hard, a conference heard on Thursday.
After decades of state-dominated economics the 1990s has seen a host of Afrian countries begin wide-ranging privatisations.

Philip Condon, deputy regional representative of privatisation consultants International Finance Corp, said unwieldy African state owned enterprises (SOEs) had to be sold off to face the modern global economy.
"The world is changing very rapidly and there is no time for any government to delay," Condon told the Southern Africa Trade and Investment Summit being held in Harare.
But he warned privatisation, with its inevitable streamlining of workforces, would be a political risk for any goverment.

"It remains a difficult process that has been slow to implement in Africa...privatisation and restructuring of SOEs invariably involves eliminating jobs and cutting subsidies -- actions that can cost governments support," he said.

Many market eyes are on South Africa's proposed privatisation programme. As the largest regional power in southern Africa many analysts hope rapid progress there will encourage quicker economic reform in the rest of southern Africa.
But South Africa's privatisation has been criticised for being too slow, though recently an international short-list was announced for a strategic stake in sprawling telecommunications giant Telkom.

Stella Sigcau, South Africa's minister of public enterprise, said there was no doubt over the government's commitment to the privatisation process. "The process has started and there is no turning back," she said.

On Wednesday, Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe said Africa's privatisations should be used to empower local black groups and Sigcau said South Africa would follow that route. The Telkom sale already includes 10 percent to be offered to black investors.
"At the heart of our programme is a commitment to the empowerment of the historically disadvantaged sector of our society, which in our case happens to be black," she said.

But Valentine Chitalu, chief executive of the Zambian privatisation agency, said the level of black ownership was a distracting issue and it was more important that a company's activities benefitted blacks. "It is important to look beyond the mere ownership of shares," he said.

Zambia's privatisation has been one of the most radical in Africa and has seen its economy, that in 1991 was 80 percent state-owned, transformed into a free market. More than 140 companies have been sold off and the whole scheme is set to be complete within three years.
Chitalu is a bullish free marketeer and believes other African countries should follow Zambia's all-out privatisation path.
"We have no such thing as a sacred cow...government should get out of the business of business and get on with better things," he said.
